title: Sealed network deployment + offline update protocol intake - Odin Healthcare
summary: Introductory discovery for a fully sealed (no egress/ingress) on-prem Redwood deployment. Customer outlined strict offline update requirements, hardware heterogeneity (older T4/RTX nodes plus small A100 pool), signed bundle delivery and chain-of-custody for updates, integration constraints with their restricted Kubernetes distribution, and compliance needs (SOC2/ISO, FIPS/KMS). Redwood AE/SE described options: fully air-gapped private control plane bundle, signed artifacts and verification, image registry import workflow, and recommended pilot scope.
topics: offline update procedure: signed bundles, removable media, chain-of-custody
hardware inventory: mixed GPUs (T4, RTX6000, single A100 nodes), memory and NVMe limits
integration with restricted Kubernetes distro and private registries
compliance and audit needs: SOC2, FIPS, HSM/KMS, image signing
action_items: Maya Patel: send sealed-network private deployment checklist + signed-bundle workflow doc - due 2026-05-26
Ethan Cruz: prepare a short tech note on image signing and verification including supported hash algorithms and example manifests - due 2026-05-27
Rajiv Menon: share HW inventory spreadsheet (GPU model, memory, NVMe, NIC) and current scheduler details - due 2026-05-25
next_steps: Schedule 60-min technical deep dive with customer infra team to map their kube distro to Redwood operator (week of 2026-05-31)
Provision a sealed-demo bundle and provide MD5/SHA signatures for offline import test (Redwood to deliver sample by 2026-05-29)
Odin to nominate pilot cluster (1 A100 node or 3 T4/RTX pooled) and provide access window for on-site engineer if needed
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-22
Start (UTC): 16:00
Duration: 55 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Ethan Cruz (Redwood SE), Dr. Lena Sf8rensen (CTO, Odin Healthcare), Rajiv Menon (Infrastructure Lead), Sabrina Cole (Head of Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen may be imperfect):
Maya opens, quick intros, then customer goes through sealed-network requirements and update rules. Discussion of hardware constraints - mixed fleet, some newer A100 but most nodes are older T4/RTX. Redwood SE explains sealed bundle, image signing, local registry import, checksum verification and offline KV-cache persistence. Customer asks about rollback, emergency patching protocols, and audit trails. End with clear next steps and pilot ask.

Topics: sealed network, offline updates, artifact signing, hardware mapping, compliance checks, pilot scope.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everybody, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, i'm the account lead here, uh we'll have Ethan our solutions engineer join in on the deep bits. Could we do quick intros?
[00:12] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Yep, lena here, CTO at Odin, i run platform and our regulated AI initiatives.
[00:17] Rajiv Menon: Rajiv - infra. I manage the clusters and hardware procurement.
[00:20] Sabrina Cole: Sabrina, security. I own compliance and audit.
[00:24] Maya Patel: Great, quick agenda: sealed-network constraints, update flow, hardware inventory, compliance, then nail down next steps. Sound good?
[00:31] All: yes / yep.
[00:34] Ethan Cruz: Quick ask from me: what's "sealed" for you? full no-egress? occasional vetted egress?
[00:40] Sabrina Cole: It's fully sealed; no outbound to external registries or control planes. The only way software or model updates happen is via physically transported media and an approved chain-of-custody.
[00:50] Maya Patel: Understood. So we're talking about a fully air-isolated cluster, we'll use the term "sealed-network" here. We support a few patterns for that, but important to map your sign-off and HSM rules.
[01:02] Rajiv Menon: We run a restricted K8s distribution - kubelet can't talk to the internet, our internal repo is on a private registry behind a firewall. Some nodes are on a different VLAN with no egress.
[01:12] Ethan Cruz: Okay that's common. Our sealed deployment option ships a signed bundle: container images, model weights, and a manifest with checksums and signatures. The operator can import the bundle from a local registry or a mounted media. The key is verifying the signature with your KMS or HSM - do you have an HSM?
[01:29] Sabrina Cole: We use an HSM and require FIPS-validated algorithms, we also need offline attestation so the bundle has to be signed by our key and by Redwood.
[01:38] Maya Patel: We can support dual-signing; Redwood can sign the artifacts and we can include instructions for validating via your HSM. We'll detail supported sig algos in the doc.
[01:46] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Hardware - we have 2x A100 nodes in the east cluster, about 8 nodes with T4s and 3 RTX6000s. Memory on several nodes is limited - 32GB RAM on the older boxes, NVMe about 1TB on each. Bandwidth constrained on some links. Does Redwood require uniform GPUs?
[02:06] Ethan Cruz: No, our runtime can run heterogenous clusters. Performance varies; for latency-sensitive routes we recommend A100/80GB or similar, but you can batch on T4s/RTX. We can also supply quantization profiles for smaller GPUs to keep model fit. That said, seq-length, batch size and KV cache interplay will affect per-token latency.
[02:23] Rajiv Menon: Our scheduler's Slurm-like but we expose k8s through a restricted wrapper. Installing a Redwood operator means we need to run it without external egress or any auto-update components.
[02:34] Ethan Cruz: That's fine - operator has an optional offline mode. In that mode, there's no heartbeat to a Redwood control plane. We provide a signed operator image and a signed manifest. Updates are applied by operator when an operator-admin imports the new manifest.
[02:46] Sabrina Cole: Hypothetical emergency: if there's a severe security fix, we need a process for expedited patching. How would that look if we have to ship a USB or encrypted SSD?
[02:56] Maya Patel: Two options: 1) Redwood prepares an emergency bundle signed and times-stamped; ship via secure courier with chain-of-custody docs and a contact window where we also provide checksums and verify receipt, or 2) temporary, restricted egress through an audited jump host under your control to pull a single artifact. You said no egress; the courier-signed bundle is more likely.
[03:15] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Courier only. The jump host idea won't pass audit.
[03:19] Ethan Cruz: Understood. For courier-signed bundles we recommend including manifest metadata: SHA-256 hashes for images and model weights, signature blocks with signing certificate chain, and a human-readable change-log. Operator will validate hashes before install.
[03:33] Rajiv Menon: Do you support storing KV cache to local persistent disks for restarts? Our workloads are batch-heavy and we can't afford warm-start penalties.
[03:41] Ethan Cruz: Yes, we support local KV cache persistence. We'll need to map where the cache sits, permissions, and ensure it survives node drain/eviction in your scheduler. In sealed setups, preffs we keep cache on encrypted NVMe (we can document recommended encryption in transit and at rest).
[03:58] Sabrina Cole: Audit trails - we require immutable logs for all operator actions and all model access for at least 3 years, and must integrate with our SIEM. Can Redwood export logs in a way that doesn't require outbound internet?
[04:11] Maya Patel: The operator writes logs to local syslog or a customer-provided log collector; we can package a log forwarder that the customer runs inside the sealed network to push to the internal SIEM. For longer retention we recommend the on-prem object store, and we can sign the log bundles for tamper-evidence.
[04:27] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: What about licensing and usage metering? We can't send usage telemetry outside.
[04:33] Maya Patel: Metering can be local-only for Private deployments. We'll produce an offline usage report that you can export and share with your procurement if needed. The hosted model is what sends telemetry; private sealed deployments are designed to be self-contained.
[04:45] Rajiv Menon: Will the installer require sudo/root and modify kernel modules? We have strict change control.
[04:50] Ethan Cruz: Installer requires cluster-admin rights to deploy the operator and CRDs; we try to avoid kernel module changes but if certain GPU drivers need host-level hooks we'll document them. For most Linux distros with supported NVIDIA drivers it's standard container runtime permissions only. We'll produce a runbook for change control.
[05:05] Maya Patel: Quick question for Sabrina: you mentioned FIPS and HSM. Are keys managed by your HSM entirely, or are you open to Redwood-held attestations?
[05:13] Sabrina Cole: Keys stay in our HSM. Redwood can publish public signing keys but private keys never leave our HSM. We want dual signatures though, both parties on the manifest.
[05:21] Ethan Cruz: That's doable - we can accept a customer-signed manifest and Redwood will append our sig; operator will verify both signatures. We'll add that to the tech note.
[05:29] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Bandwidth for model loads is a concern - we can't stream large model weights across internal links frequently. Can Redwood support model cache pre-warming, or pre-loads via the bundle?
[05:39] Ethan Cruz: Yes, the sealed bundle can include model shards and a preload step. Alternatively, you can have a local model registry populated once by physical media, and operator will pull from there. We can also provide quantized variants to reduce size.
[05:50] Rajiv Menon: Any known limitations with mixed T4 and A100 when running the same model?
[05:55] Ethan Cruz: You can run variants; the runtime will route requests to nodes based on model variant compatibility. Latency SLOs differ. Also KV-cache format is compatible across same model architecture but different quantization can affect output and consistency; we'll call that out in the pilot.
[06:12] Sabrina Cole: We need to see an example signed bundle and the verification steps. Also, a short threat-model: what stops an attacker with physical access to the media?
[06:22] Maya Patel: We'll include best practices: encrypted media, signed manifests, tamper-evident seals, courier chain-of-custody, HSM verification, and checksums signed by two keys. The threat-model doc will be part of the security pack.
[06:33] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Pilot ask: we'd like a minimal pilot to validate the install & offline update process — not performance tests yet. One A100 node preferred but if not available, a 3-node T4 pool is fine. Timeline: start pilot early June.
[06:47] Maya Patel: Sounds reasonable. We'll propose a pilot plan in the next doc.
[06:52] Ethan Cruz: For pilot we'll need access to your HW inventory, kube manifests for the restricted distro, and a secure window to import the sealed bundle. Also confirm who will be the operator-admin during pilot.
[07:03] Rajiv Menon: I'll be operator-admin and will share inventory.
[07:07] Sabrina Cole: I'll review security docs and compliance checklist.
[07:11] Maya Patel: Great. Quick recap and next steps?
[07:15] Maya Patel: Redwood to send sealed-network checklist, signed-bundle example, and tech note on signatures; customer to share inventory and schedule deep dive.
[07:24] Dr. Lena Sf8rensen: Correct.
[07:26] Maya Patel: Anything else?
[07:28] Rajiv Menon: One more little thing — can Redwood provide a short runbook for on-site engineers to avoid mistakes during manual import?
[07:34] Ethan Cruz: Yes we'll prepare a step-by-step runbook for manual import and rollback procedure.
[07:39] Sabrina Cole: Perfect.
[07:41] Maya Patel: Okay thanks everyone. We'll follow up via email with the artifacts. Meeting end.
